findings.description: audit/log imports jobs/reminders to call scheduleFollowUp on 'cancelled', reminders imports mailer, and mailer imports audit/log, forming a runtime cycle where an audit write has a hidden side effect of scheduling a job; decoupling (audit as a leaf, follow-up scheduling triggered by the caller or an event) would remove the cycle and the surprising coupling.

The loan status lifecycle is spread over four tiny files plus a separate LoanStatus union in shared/types and hard-coded status checks in service.isOpen and reminders ('active'), all keyed by untyped strings; one deeper loan-status module owning states, transitions, terminal-ness and labels would give a single place to change.

LoanStore exposes raw SQL WHERE fragments, LoanRow and a raw() escape hatch, so LoanService and ReminderJob each duplicate row-to-Loan mapping (fromRow vs inline) and Loan-to-row mapping three times; unlike MemberStore, a store that speaks domain Loan with intent-named queries would hide the SQL and the serialization.
Paging validation and clamping is implemented twice (middleware.paging and validation.validatePaging, each applying pageSizeMax) so a rule change must be made in both places.

LoanService.cancel sets status to 'lost' while bypassing canTransition and recording 'cancelled', and show() makes a second full load via quote(id), so lifecycle rules and the double fetch leak into service and handler instead of living behind one transition interface.

Money formatting and rounding is duplicated (pricing.formatAmount vs renderer.money, with notice total recomputed in builder from priceOf), so currency presentation and totals can drift across three modules.

Behavior depends on module-level mutable singletons (cached settings(), audit sink and memory, mail transport and outbox, pendingFollowUps, notice and loan sequence counters) which tests must reset through back doors, suggesting injected dependencies.

dispatch.ts is a 7-line wrapper that only fixes the template kind on sendTemplate; folding it into the mailer (or giving the notify module a real send-notification interface) would remove a shallow layer.

The reminder variables are built inline in ReminderJob.run while templates.reminderVars builds the same map, so the template contract lives in two places; the notify module should accept a trip and driver and build the variables itself.

The HTTP handler assembles manifests and quotes itself (fetch trip, build, render, format) and supplies the pricing 'priority' flag, which belongs to the driver tier but is never looked up; moving this behind a service method would keep pricing rules and driver tier out of the transport layer.

findings.description: The payment due date is computed four different ways: calendar days in builder.dueAt, business days in renderer.payBy, UTC weekend rollover in profile.nextPaymentDue, and local-time Sunday-only rollover in reminders.paymentDeadline. A single deep payment-terms module would stop the invoice's stored due date, its printed due date and the reminder timing from disagreeing.

customer/service imports isOpen from order/service while order/service imports isActiveCustomer from customer/service. OrderService.create also has to be handed the customer's expiry by its caller. Moving the open and active rules into a shared domain module would break the cycle and let order creation check the customer itself.

Paging rules (offset >= 0, limit > 0, clamp to max) are implemented twice, in middleware.paging and in validation.validatePaging, and both run on the same request path via OrderService.list. One owner for paging would remove the duplicate checks and the two sources of the max.

The Config class has one trivial getter per setting plus ad-hoc setters, so its interface is as wide as its data. It is also reached through a global config() singleton from many modules. Exposing the typed Settings object, injected where needed, would remove about 17 methods and the test-reset hook.

The priority-tier discount in priceOf and buildInvoice is a flag that the handlers always leave false (quote(id, false), buildInvoice(entity)). The customer's tier is never looked up, so priority pricing is unreachable. Pricing should resolve the customer tier behind one interface instead of relying on every caller to pass it.

Paging validation exists twice (middleware.paging and validatePaging, called again from TripService.list) and the page-size clamp is applied in both layers; a single owner would remove the duplication and drift risk.

Trip lifecycle knowledge (transition table, isOpen, cancel's closed-status check, the hardcoded 'en_route' in the reminder job, the status cast in toDomain) is spread across files rather than behind one status interface.

The manifest handler orchestrates build and render itself, bypassing the service, so priority pricing is never applied and manifestExported is never audited; a manifest service in front of builder and renderer would own the flow.

Module-level mutable state and ambient singletons (manifest lastNumber counter, trip id sequence, cached settings(), the global audit sink and memory, the mailer transport and outbox) are reached through import rather than passed in, so tests need reset and swap hooks and manifest numbering is also not durable across restarts.

findings.description: customer/service imports isOpen from order/service while order/service imports isActiveCustomer from customer/service (runtime cycle); moving the open/active predicates into a shared domain module, or giving them one owner, would break the cycle.

The payment due date is computed four different ways (builder: plain calendar days; renderer payBy: skips weekends using local time; profile nextPaymentDue: calendar days then weekend shift in UTC; reminders paymentDeadline: only Sunday pushed to Monday), so an invoice's dueAt, printed pay-by date and reminder deadline can disagree; one deep due-date module would own the rule.

Customer activeness is decided by isActiveCustomer, yet OrderService.create takes the customer's expiry as an optional parameter defaulting to null (always active), and the order handler never passes it, so the check is effectively bypassed; the order service should resolve the customer itself behind one interface.

Config is a class of one getter per field, mirroring the Settings interface one-to-one, plus mutable setters and a global singleton; the interface is as large as the data it wraps, and callers could take a typed Settings object instead.

Many modules call the global config() singleton inside their logic (tax rate, currency, payment term), so behaviour depends on hidden mutable global state and tests must reset it; passing settings in explicitly would make these modules testable in isolation.

Paging validation is duplicated: middleware.paging and validatePaging implement the same offset/limit rules and clamp to the page-size max, and OrderService.list re-validates what the handler already validated; the pure validators are separate from the call sites where bad input slips through (validateNewOrder does not check types of items from raw JSON, and validateId/validateNote are unused).

The priority tier is a Customer attribute, but handlers call quote(id,false) and buildInvoice(entity) with the default priority=false, so the priority discount is never applied through HTTP; callers must remember to look up and thread the flag instead of the pricing flow owning it.

Router.statusOf re-implements error-to-status mapping by instanceof while shared/errors already has isDomainError; the error-to-HTTP mapping lives in the router rather than with the errors, and the Handler type omits headers that order handlers return.

Invoice numbers come from an in-process counter (lastNumber) and order ids from a module-level sequence, so identifier generation resets on restart and is not tied to storage; no store owns uniqueness.

findings.description: Paging rules (offset/limit checks, clamping to pageSizeMax) are implemented twice, in validatePaging and in middleware paging(), so a rule change must be made in both places; consolidating into one paging module would give one place for the rule.

Money rounding and display is spread over four modules with conflicting rules (round in pricing and builder, truncate in displayAmount, toFixed in renderer money, formatAmount in pricing), so the same total can display differently; one money module would own rounding and formatting.

Bill total is recomputed in builder.ts from subtotal, discount and tax instead of using the total from priceOf, and priceOf's total expression (taxable + tax * 100) / 100 has misplaced precedence, so the two totals can diverge; the bill should take its figures from a single pricing result.

Handlers call the domain in several steps and apply domain rules themselves (show quotes separately, bill builds and exports from the HTTP layer, patient show computes activity via isActivePatient); the priority tier is never passed to pricing, so deepening the services would move these rules behind them.

export.ts only dispatches on format to renderer functions, borrowing the renderer's parameter type, and its interface is as large as its body; folding format selection and content type into the renderer would remove a module.
PatientProfile is a getter/setter wrapper over fields of a plain Patient object with a trivial displayName helper; its interface is as large as the data it wraps, so removing it would reduce surface.
record is a pure pass-through to the private write, and the module-level mutable sink and memory state keep it hard to isolate in tests.

Business logic reads global settings() and module-level mutable state (bill numbers, mail transport, follow-up set, audit sink), so tests need global reset hooks, and no module has any test importing it; passing config and collaborators explicitly would make them testable.

The router hand-lists ten routes with duplicated id regexes and its own error-to-status mapping, which duplicates isDomainError in shared/errors, so adding an endpoint or error kind touches several places.

Lifecycle rules are split: transition uses the TRANSITIONS table, cancel re-checks status by hand and isOpen repeats the same status knowledge, and validateNote duplicates the note rules in validateNewAppointment.

findings.description: LoanGateway only forwards find/list/save to LoanStore with no added behaviour, so LoanService could depend on LoanStore directly (or the gateway should absorb real behaviour) and drop a layer.

Notice numbering is split into four 3-8 line modules that builder.ts must chain together (prefix, sequence, pad, format); folding them into one deep numbering module with a single nextNoticeNumber(issuedAt) interface would give locality and one place to test and reset the sequence.

MemberStore returns raw QueryResult/MemberRow, so MemberService and ReminderJob each check rowCount, read snake_case columns and (in service) map rows to Member, duplicating the not-found and row-mapping logic three times; the store should return domain Member or throw NotFoundError as LoanStore does.

Paging validation and clamping is implemented twice (middleware.paging and validation.validatePaging, both applied via service.list) with the same rules and page-size settings, so a rule change must be made in two places.

Member rules are spread out: input validation lives in the handler while normalisation is in the service, and active/expiry logic (isActiveMember) lives in the service yet is called from the handler, with profile.ts holding display logic; a member module owning validation and activity would give locality.

Validation duplicates the price rule (unitPrice finite and non-negative) that pricing.assertPriced also enforces, and validateId/validateNote are exported but unused by the service; the loan rules are scattered across modules instead of behind one interface.

Priority pricing is decided by callers (handler passes false, builder defaults false) rather than derived from the member's tier, so the discount rule leaks into every call site and the show handler and notice builder can disagree on totals.

The reminder job must know template variable shape (reminderVars) and compose lookup, vars and send itself; a single notify interface like sendReminder(loan, member) would hide the template and vars details.

Module-level pendingFollowUps state in reminders.ts is global and written by scheduleFollowUp without being tied to the job instance, and scheduler computes the reminder interval from reminderLeadDays, coupling unrelated settings to schedule cadence.

findings.description: The customer's priority tier lives on Customer, but pricing takes a `priority` boolean that callers must supply: `quote(id,false)` is hard-coded, and `buildInvoice` defaults to false and is called without it. The priority discount is never applied in the real flow. A deeper pricing module that resolves the customer's tier itself would put the rule in one place.

Paging rules (offset >= 0, limit > 0, clamp to pageSizeMax) are implemented twice, in `middleware.paging` and `validatePaging`, with the default and max coming from settings in each. Owning them in one module would remove the duplicated checks and the possibility of drift.

Order lifecycle knowledge is split. The TRANSITIONS table governs `transition`, but `cancel` hard-codes its own closed-status check and bypasses the table, and `isOpen` encodes a third view. The 'cancelled' notification template exists but nothing sends it. Adding a status means touching all of these, so a single lifecycle module would help.

Module-level mutable state (the invoice counter `lastNumber`, the audit memory, the mail outbox, the cached settings) sits behind functions with no injection point. Invoice numbers restart on every process start and tests cannot isolate state. Injectable numbering and sink dependencies would fix both.

The router's `Handler` type is `{status, body}`, while order handlers return a `Response` that includes headers, and customer handlers repeat the inline shape. Headers survive only through a spread at runtime. A single shared response type, plus error-to-status mapping built on `isDomainError`, would tighten the seam.

Money formatting exists twice: `formatAmount` in pricing rounds, but the renderer's private `money` does not. Both append the currency from settings. One formatter would keep amounts rendered consistently.

findings.description: Paging rules (offset >= 0, limit > 0, clamp to pageSizeMax) are implemented twice, in middleware.paging() and validation.validatePaging(), and both run on the same request path (handler then OrderService.list), so one policy change must be made in two places; a single paging module owning parse, validate and clamp would remove the duplicate.

The priority-customer discount is a pricing input passed as a bare boolean, but every caller (order-handlers.show via quote(id,false), invoice() via buildInvoice default) hard-codes false and never derives it from Customer.tier, so priority pricing is unreachable; the invoice builder also recomputes the total instead of using price.total, so a pricing module that resolves the customer tier and returns the full breakdown would own this rule in one place.

reminderLeadDays means both the staleness cutoff in ReminderJob.run and, times 60, the scheduler's run interval in reminderJob(), and scheduleFollowUp() adds ids to pendingFollowUps that run() only ever deletes, never processes, so the follow-up promise in its doc comment is not implemented; the reminder concept (cadence, cutoff, follow-ups) should live behind one job interface.

The reminder job must know the template kind 'reminder' and separately import reminderVars from templates and sendTemplate from mailer, so the caller assembles a template/variable pairing that the notify module could own behind something like sendReminder(order, customer).

The order lifecycle is expressed three ways in one module: the TRANSITIONS table, a hand-written closed-status check in cancel() that bypasses the table (and so sets a note that transition(…,'cancelled') does not), and isOpen(); folding these into one state-machine interface would keep the rules consistent.

Customer expiry semantics are split: isActiveCustomer with its grace period lives in the service, the handler composes it with profileView, profile formats expiresAt, and the store's expiringBefore ignores the grace period, so 'active' has no single owner.

findings.description: customer/service imports isOpen from order/service while order/service imports isActiveCustomer from customer/service (runtime cycle); moving the customer-activity and order-open predicates into a shared domain module, or passing the customer in, would break the loop.

The payment due date rule is implemented four times with different semantics (profile.nextPaymentDue skips weekends using UTC, renderer.payBy counts business days in local time, reminders.paymentDeadline only skips Sunday, builder.dueAt uses plain calendar days), so the printed due date can differ from the stored dueAt and reminder timing; one payment-terms module would give a single rule.

Customer activity (expiry plus grace) is decided in customer/service but OrderService.create takes a customerExpiry parameter defaulting to null, so the order-handler path never supplies it and inactive customers can place orders; the rule should live behind one interface that order creation actually consults.

Paging validation is duplicated in middleware.paging and validation.validatePaging (same rules and clamping), and the handler passes raw input to the service which re-validates, so the HTTP and domain layers both own the rule.

Config is a class of one-getter-per-field wrappers plus setters over a Settings object, behind a hidden global config() singleton read directly by many modules; its interface is as large as its content and makes dependent logic hard to test without resetConfigForTests, so passing the needed values in would be simpler.

Module-level mutable state (audit memory and sink, mail outbox and transport, invoice lastNumber counter, order id sequence) is swapped via setters or not at all, so tests share state and invoice numbering is not durable or injectable.

Router's statusOf maps error classes to HTTP codes by duplicating the list that shared/errors isDomainError already encodes, and the Response type is defined in order-handlers while the router redeclares its own handler shape, so the error-to-status and response contract has no single home.

findings.description: export.ts is a 7-line wrapper that only switches between renderText/renderHtml and maps format to content-type; folding format selection and content-type into the renderer (one render(bill, format) returning body and contentType) removes a module and the Parameters<typeof renderText> type trick.

Money rounding and formatting is duplicated with divergent rules (pricing.formatAmount rounds, renderer.money uses toFixed, handlers.displayAmount truncates, builder recomputes total with EPSILON rounding), so a displayed total can disagree with the bill; one money module would own rounding and formatting.

priceOf computes total as Math.round(taxable + tax * 100) / 100 (misplaced parenthesis) giving a wrong total, which is why builder.ts ignores price.total and recomputes it; having pricing return a correct total and builder consume it would remove the duplicated calculation.
Paging validation and clamping is implemented twice (middleware.paging and validation.validatePaging) with the same rules and separate use of settings, so a rule change must be made in both places.

The notion of an open or stale appointment is spread across service.isOpen, the cancel status check that duplicates TRANSITIONS, and the reminder job's hard-coded 'checked_in' staleness query, so lifecycle rules live in several places.

PatientProfile is a getter/setter-per-field wrapper whose interface mirrors the Patient fields one-for-one and adds no behaviour; it is used only to read fields in the handler and to get a name in displayName, so it could be deleted in favour of the plain Patient type.

The patient handler validates input shape, computes activity via isActivePatient and assembles the response itself, so business rules (grace period, required fields) leak into the HTTP layer while the service lacks validation, unlike the appointment service which validates internally.

Module-level mutable singletons (audit sink and memory, mail transport and outbox, bill number counter, appointment id sequence, pending follow-ups) are reached through direct imports, so services cannot be given isolated collaborators and tests share hidden state.

connection.ts pulls global settings for connectionString and withStatementTimeout issues SET LOCAL outside any guarantee of a transaction, so the Db interface does not own its configuration or transaction semantics.

findings.description: audit/log imports jobs/reminders (scheduleFollowUp on 'cancelled'), reminders imports mailer, and mailer imports audit/log: a runtime cycle where recording an audit entry triggers job scheduling; moving the follow-up trigger out of the audit log (e.g. into LoanService.cancel) or making the audit sink side-effect free would break it.

The loan lifecycle (states, transitions, terminal, label) is spread over four tiny one-function files that take plain strings, duplicate the state list with LoanStatus in shared/types, and are paired by hand in service.ts (isState && canTransition); also service.isOpen and cancel's hard-coded 'lost' repeat the rules. One deep loan-status module would own the state machine behind a typed interface.

Row-to-Loan mapping (fromRow) and Loan-to-row serialization are duplicated in service.ts (three upsert blocks plus fromRow) and again inline in reminders.ts, while LoanStore only exposes raw SQL fragments and LoanRow; MemberStore by contrast returns domain objects. Making LoanStore take and return Loan (findById, save, listByStatus) would remove the duplication and the load-by-id/NotFound boilerplate repeated in get/transition/cancel/quote.

LoanStore.select/count accept caller-written SQL WHERE and suffix strings (including interpolated LIMIT/OFFSET) and expose raw(), so callers must know column names and SQL syntax; the store's interface is nearly as complex as the SQL it wraps.

Cancelling a loan 'cancelled' audit entry is what triggers scheduleFollowUp, and sendTemplate records a 'reminded' audit with a loan entity type regardless of template; the audit log carries business side-effects, and cancel() also sets status 'lost' rather than a cancelled state, so action names and behaviour disagree.

Paging validation is implemented twice (middleware.paging and validation.validatePaging, with the max clamp in both) and input validation is split between handlers (member register checks) and loan/validation; validation of member input lives nowhere central, so rule changes touch several layers.

Money handling is spread out: formatAmount in pricing and a separate money() in renderer both format with currency, builder recomputes total from price parts, and the handler's show quotes with priority=false while notice never passes priority; a single money/pricing module would keep rounding and currency rules in one place.

Pure-looking logic reads the global settings() singleton and module-level mutable state (notice counter, pendingFollowUps, audit memory, mail outbox, transport) instead of receiving them, so tests need resetSettingsForTests and global swapping.

findings.description: pricing.ts imports describeLine from bill/builder while builder imports priceOf, lineTotal, roundMoney and pricedLines from pricing, a runtime cycle; moving line labelling to one side (or pricing/line wording into a single module) would break it.

ReminderJob hand-assembles the RFC 5322 headers, retries 4xx replies, and interprets 550/553 codes itself, so SMTP protocol knowledge leaks out of the mailer; a deeper sendTemplated(to, kind, vars) interface would hide it and make the job testable without SMTP details.

Paging validation (non-negative integer offset, positive limit, clamp to pageSizeMax) is implemented in both middleware.paging and validation.validatePaging, which service.list re-runs, so the rules can drift.

Request validation is inconsistent: the status in move, reason in cancel, and the id path pattern are checked in none of the validation module, while validateId and validateNote are never called by the service or handlers, so the validation module's interface is only partially in use.

Business rules sit apart from where they are used: isOpen in appointment/service and isActivePatient in patient/service are exported pure helpers with the handler computing 'active' itself, and appointment cancel duplicates the TRANSITIONS rule with its own status check instead of going through it.
